transcript.text: Thank you, Elena. Here's my coverage analysis on the vendor-breach endorsement. I reviewed the endorsement this morning — the carrier's coverage file came in shortly before this meeting, which is why I hadn't circulated it yet. The critical finding is this: under the cyber policy's vendor-breach endorsement, this claim qualifies for coverage only if the formal tender identifies the event as a vendor-breach privacy claim. The complaint alleges that account information was exposed through a software vendor's compromised credentials, which aligns with the vendor-breach trigger — but if the tender is not properly characterized as a vendor-breach privacy claim, we risk losing coverage entirely. This directly intersects with everything we've heard today: Nadia's carrier claims note with the $900,000 settlement authority and mediation-first sequence would only be available to us if the tender is correctly structured to trigger the vendor-breach endorsement. Jordan's confidential-resolution directive with no admission of wrongdoing needs to be carefully balanced against the requirement to identify the event as a vendor-breach privacy claim in the tender — we can characterize the nature of the event for coverage purposes without admitting wrongdoing. And Maya's conflicts findings on counsel selection matter because whoever handles the defense and mediation will need to be aligned with this tender structure from the outset. Elena, I'm recommending that the response package include a formally structured tender that explicitly identifies this as a vendor-breach privacy claim under the endorsement, so that the coverage — and by extension the carrier's $900,000 authority and mediation-first sequence — is preserved.

transcript.text: Thank you, Elena. Here are my conflicts findings. I completed my conflict check late yesterday after receiving the proposed insurer panel firm name. The check revealed that the proposed panel firm currently represents the lead plaintiff's employer in an unrelated but active matter. This creates a direct conflict of interest that disqualifies that firm from serving as our defense counsel in this matter. As a result, the company must appoint independent defense counsel rather than using the insurer's proposed panel firm. I have not yet issued my written clearance because of this finding. This has significant implications for everything we've heard today: the independent counsel we select will need to handle the mediation the carrier is requiring under Nadia's claims note, will need to structure the tender in line with Thomas's vendor-breach endorsement recommendation, and will need to pursue the confidential resolution with no admission of wrongdoing that Jordan described. I'm recommending that the response package include appointment of independent defense counsel and that we initiate the selection process immediately so we can move forward with the tender and mediation sequence.
